title: Scientists Track Down Missing Matter Hiding Around Galaxies
summary:
For years, scientists have calculated how much matter should exist in the universe. But more than half of the ordinary matter did not seem to show up in telescope images. Now researchers say some of it is hiding in huge, faint clouds of gas around galaxies.

This missing matter is called ordinary because it is made of everyday particles, like the protons and neutrons that make up stars, planets and people. It is different from dark matter, a mysterious substance that does not give off, reflect or absorb light.

"The missing matter exists as a thin gas that's very spread out," said Haochen Wang, a PhD student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who led the new study. In some places, there is less than one proton or electron in a space about the size of a washing machine. That makes it very hard to find.

To search for it, Wang's team used fast radio bursts, or FRBs. These are very strong flashes of radio waves from far away that last about one-thousandth of a second. As an FRB travels toward Earth, it passes through gas. The gas slows longer radio waves a bit more than shorter ones, a little like a prism splitting light into a rainbow. The more gas the signal passes through, the more stretched out it becomes when it reaches telescopes.

By measuring this stretching, Wang's team measured how far gas typically spreads around galaxies. They say it is the first definitive detection of the missing ordinary matter. The study appeared in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Not everyone agrees it is the first. Astronomer Vikram Ravi of Caltech said earlier work hinted at the gas, and some numbers could be off. Still, he called the study "a great signpost of what is to come."
why_it_matters: Finding the missing ordinary matter helps scientists check whether their picture of how the universe is built is correct.

background_read: Everything we can see, from people to planets to stars, is made of atoms built from particles such as protons, neutrons and electrons.
Astronomers can estimate how much ordinary matter should exist in the universe, but much of it has been hard to spot because it does not shine brightly.
Radio waves are a kind of light our eyes cannot see, and telescopes can detect them coming from very distant places in space.
When light or radio waves pass through gas, the gas can change the signal slightly, which lets scientists learn about matter they cannot see directly.
